title: DLLs and Modular Programs
tagline: Build, export, load and version your own libraries on Windows
description: Everything about dynamic-link libraries in your own software: exporting functions and classes, import libraries, run-time loading, the loader and its search order, DllMain and its rules, designing stable interfaces across versions, plugin systems and hot reloading during development. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course. You build the real DLLs in Visual Studio; the practice on the site checks the logic behind each idea.

milestones.title: DLL Foundations
milestones.blurb: What a DLL is, what the Windows loader does with it, and how to build, export from and link against your first one.

lessons.title: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
lessons.summary: A **dynamic-link library** is compiled code that is not part of your `.exe` but is joined to it when the program starts or while it runs. This lesson explains what a DLL contains, how it differs from a static library, and the real reasons programs are split into them, along with the costs.

lessons.title: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
lessons.summary: Before `main` runs, the Windows **loader** finds every DLL the program needs, maps each one into memory once, loads their own dependencies, fixes up addresses and fills in the program's tables of function addresses. Knowing these steps explains most "DLL not found" and "entry point not found" errors.

lessons.title: Your First DLL in Visual Studio
lessons.summary: Build a DLL and a program that uses it, in one Visual Studio solution. You meet the **export macro** pattern that lets one header serve both the library and the programs using it, and see where the `.dll` and its import `.lib` end up.

lessons.title: Exporting Functions and Data
lessons.summary: There are two ways to say what a DLL exports, `__declspec(dllexport)` and a **module-definition file** (`.def`). This lesson covers both, plus **ordinals**, exporting variables, and what goes into the export table.

lessons.title: Import Libraries and Load-Time Linking
lessons.summary: When a program links against a DLL's **import library**, the linker writes an **import table** into the program and calls go through the **import address table**, which the loader fills in. This lesson follows one call from your source code to the DLL.

lessons.title: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
lessons.summary: When a program will not start or calls the wrong thing, you need to see what a module exports, what it imports, and where each DLL really came from. This lesson covers `dumpbin`, the Dependencies tool, the debugger's Modules window and Process Monitor.

milestones.title: Across the Boundary
milestones.blurb: Names, calling conventions, loading at run time, DllMain, and the things that must never cross from one module to another: memory, exceptions and C++ library types.

lessons.title: Name Mangling and extern "C"
lessons.summary: C++ lets two functions share a name if their parameters differ, so the compiler gives every function a **decorated** name that encodes its parameter types. Those names are what a DLL exports by default. `extern "C"` turns decoration off, giving the plain names that `GetProcAddress`, `.def` files and other languages need.

lessons.title: Calling Conventions at the Boundary
lessons.summary: A **calling convention** is the agreement about where a function's arguments go and who cleans up afterwards. On 64-bit Windows there is essentially one; on 32-bit Windows there are several, and they change the exported name. Getting the convention wrong across a DLL boundary corrupts the stack.

lessons.title: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
lessons.summary: Instead of linking against an import library, a program can load a DLL whenever it likes with `LoadLibraryW`, look up functions by name with `GetProcAddress`, call them through function pointers, and unload the DLL with `FreeLibrary`. This is the foundation of plugins and hot reload.

tasks.title: Look it up or say why

lessons.title: DllMain and the Loader Lock
lessons.summary: A DLL can have an entry point, `DllMain`, that Windows calls when the DLL is loaded and unloaded and when threads start and end. It runs while the loader holds a lock, which makes most interesting work inside it dangerous. This lesson shows what DllMain is for, what it must never do, and what to do instead.

lessons.title: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
lessons.summary: Memory allocated in one module and freed in another can crash, because each module may have its **own copy of the C runtime and its own heap**. The fix is a simple rule: whoever allocates, frees. This lesson shows why it breaks and the standard patterns that keep it safe.

lessons.title: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
lessons.summary: Besides memory, two other things must not cross a stable DLL boundary - **exceptions** and **C++ library types** such as `std::string`. This lesson shows what goes wrong, the "exception barrier" that turns exceptions into error codes at the edge of a DLL, and the rare case where exporting C++ types is fine.

milestones.title: Stable Interfaces
milestones.blurb: Designing a library other code can rely on for years: opaque handles, error reporting, versioned structs, COM-style interfaces and version numbers that mean something.

lessons.title: Designing a Stable C Interface
lessons.summary: A library that other programs depend on for years needs an interface that can grow without breaking them. The standard shape is a set of `extern "C"` functions around **opaque handles**, with a consistent naming scheme and clear ownership. This lesson designs one from scratch and lists the rules that keep it stable.

lessons.title: Error Reporting Across a C API
lessons.summary: A C interface reports failure with **result codes**, but a code alone rarely tells a developer what went wrong. This lesson designs a result enum that can grow, adds a **thread-local last error message** like `GetLastError`, and shows how callers should handle codes they have never seen.

lessons.title: Versioned Structs and Function Tables
lessons.summary: Sometimes callers need to see a struct, such as an options block. Windows' trick is to start every such struct with its own **size**, so the library can tell which version the caller was built with. The same idea, applied to a struct full of function pointers, gives a **function table** that can grow across versions.

lessons.title: COM-Style Interfaces with vtables
lessons.summary: A C interface can still give callers **objects with methods**, if the object's layout is just a pointer to a table of functions. On Windows, an abstract C++ class with only virtual functions has exactly that layout, which is how COM, DirectX and many plugin systems work. This lesson builds a COM-style interface with reference counting and `QueryInterface`.

lessons.title: Versioning and Compatibility
lessons.summary: A version number is a promise about compatibility. **Semantic versioning** turns that promise into rules: major for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. This lesson applies it to DLLs, shows how a program checks the version it got at run time, and covers side-by-side installs for breaking changes.

lessons.title: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++
lessons.summary: A stable C interface is pleasant for the DLL and other languages, but tedious to use from C++. The answer is a thin **header-only C++ wrapper** on the caller's side - RAII classes that create and destroy handles, exceptions instead of result codes, `std::string` instead of buffers - while the DLL boundary stays pure C.

milestones.title: Loading Safely and Shipping
milestones.blurb: Where Windows looks for a DLL and how to make sure it finds yours, delay loading, version resources, runtimes, and choosing between static libraries and DLLs.

lessons.title: The DLL Search Order
lessons.summary: When a program asks for a DLL by name rather than by full path, Windows tries a fixed list of places. Knowing that list explains why the wrong copy of a DLL sometimes loads, why "it works on my machine", and why putting your DLLs next to your `.exe` is the reliable choice.

lessons.title: Loading Only the Files You Mean
lessons.summary: Loading a DLL by bare name leaves the choice of file to the search order, which an attacker or an accident can influence. This lesson shows how to load exactly the file you intend - full paths, `SetDefaultDllDirectories`, `AddDllDirectory` and the `LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_*` flags - and how to check a plugin folder before loading anything from it.

lessons.title: Delay Loading
lessons.summary: **Delay loading** gives you the convenience of linking against an import library with the timing of run-time loading. The DLL is loaded the first time one of its functions is called, not when the program starts. This lesson shows how to turn it on, what happens on the first call, and how to handle a DLL that turns out to be missing.

lessons.title: Version Resources, Runtimes and Shipping
lessons.summary: Getting a program with DLLs onto someone else's computer means three things - giving each file a **version resource** so people and installers can tell versions apart, making sure the **Visual C++ runtime** is there (or not needed), and laying out the files so the search order finds the right ones.

lessons.title: Static Libraries, DLLs or Header-Only
lessons.summary: You now know what DLLs cost and what they give. This lesson compares the three ways to package reusable C++ code - header-only, static library, DLL - and gives a short set of questions for choosing, with examples from real projects.

milestones.title: Plugins and Hot Reload
milestones.blurb: Two of the best reasons to use DLLs in your own programs: a plugin system that loads code you did not ship, and reloading game code while the game keeps running.

lessons.title: A Plugin System
lessons.summary: A plugin system lets your program load DLLs it was never built with - written later, by you or by players making mods. This lesson designs one for a game - a plugin folder, one required export, an API version check, an interface the host gives to the plugin, and clean loading and unloading - using everything from milestones 2 to 4.

lessons.title: A Plugin Registry and Capabilities
lessons.summary: Once several plugins are loaded, the host needs to know what each one provides - new stone types, weather effects, console commands - and route requests to the right one. This lesson builds a **registry** that plugins register into during `start`, handles name clashes and dependencies between plugins, and cleans up everything a plugin registered when it unloads.

tasks.title: A registry that cleans up after plugins

lessons.title: Hot Reloading Code
lessons.summary: Hot reloading means changing game code, rebuilding, and having the **running** game pick up the new code within a second, without restarting or losing your place. The trick is to put gameplay code in a DLL and swap it. This lesson covers the loop - watch, copy, unload, load - and the problems each step solves.

lessons.title: Keeping State Across a Reload
lessons.summary: Hot reload is only useful if the game keeps its state - the player's position, the enemies, the score - while the code changes. This lesson shows the two strategies, **host-owned memory** and **save and restore**, and how to handle the hard case: a reload that changes the layout of the state itself.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Moddable Game
lessons.summary: Bring the whole course together in one Visual Studio solution - a small game whose gameplay hot-reloads while it runs, and which loads plugins that add new content through a versioned C interface. This lesson is the plan, the checklist and the order to build it in.
